title: Breaking and Entering: Jamie xx
summary: During the Melbourne portion of his Australian tour, Jamie xx joins Simon and Lauren on Breaking and Entering to chat about his latest record In Waves, as well as his collaborators and more.
transcript:
Jamie xx joined Simon Winkler and Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studios on 5 December 2024 during his Australian tour, to discuss his latest album In Waves. A founding member of The xx and a DJ and producer, he combines UK dance music traditions with innovative production techniques. Released nearly a decade after his debut In Colour, In Waves features an array of collaborators and draws on his experience of dance culture around the world. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Welcome back to Australia, and to Triple R.

Jamie: Good to be back.

Simon: We were delighted to enjoy some guest program selections the last time you were here. And we understand that beyond Triple R, you have some pretty deep connections to Australia: lots of friends here, and increasingly some surfing places you like to go. Is that right?

Jamie: Yeah. I've been coming here for like 15 years, almost every year, which is great. I love it. It kind of feels like a second home sometimes. I've made loads of pals in Melbourne, Sydney and Byron, so we usually manage to do some kind of side party, beach doof thing. I love it.

Simon: We do want to talk more about the place of surfing in your life later on. But perhaps we could begin with In Waves, a different kind of wave, of course. The album came together over a number of years, and we were interested in the story of the record, and the place of patience, of allowing things to unfold. Could you talk about that?

Jamie: I definitely wasn't patient for a long time. After In Colour, I wanted to make an album pretty much immediately, and I was always making music, with the band and for other people. But I guess because I'd been doing this for so long, the same thing over and over again, touring, coming to Australia every year, which is all amazing stuff, I kind of lost the enjoyment of making the music, because it was about the end game rather than the process. So I just had to find that again. During lockdown, I got the chance to go home and be at home for a long period of time, for the first time ever, really. I started making music again and actually really enjoying it, not thinking about when it would come out or when people would hear it. It was just such a pleasure.

Lauren: Was there a clear point when you started to understand what the album was about, and what story it would tell?

Jamie: Pretty early on, actually. When I started enjoying the music-making process again, the first couple of things I made were 'Dafodil' and 'Breather' from the record. They both had similar things in them, which was sort of spoken word: a way I could get some of my thoughts across without actually having to put my voice in it. And when you're making a record, it's all about finding these sorts of limitations that you can work within, and then building something from that. So that was a good starting point.

Simon: How many songs didn't make it onto the record?

Jamie: So many. But I'm very slow at making music, so nothing that didn't make the record got finished. I just spent a long, long time finishing these tracks, and actually the longest time ever tracklisting it, so it felt like a perfect album listen. That's still very important to me, even though I think a lot of people don't listen to music that way these days.

Lauren: I think it's a beautiful thing, to preserve the idea of a sequenced set of songs. We read that your friend Kieran Hebden, aka Four Tet, helped you sequence the songs. How did he help you put the puzzle together?

Jamie: I always try and enlist friends I trust to give me some perspective. Especially when you're making a record on your own, it can get to the point where you lose all perspective and you're just bouncing ideas around in your own head. I'd been playing a lot of these songs out over the years, testing them on crowds, changing things depending on how they were working. So I had an idea of what I wanted to do with the tracklist, but as I was putting it together, I just couldn't get it right, because obviously it's totally different to playing a show, even though I'd kind of worked out an order for live.

Simon: On that idea of songs developing in response to audience reactions, could you give us an example of how a song might be adapted based on how an audience reacts?

Jamie: Well, you can really feel it in a room. You can feel the energy levels drop and rise, and the benefit of being a DJ is that I can just stand there and watch them. We've done that as a band with The xx, playing new songs before they've been released, but you're concentrating so hard on not messing up that you can't really gauge anything except getting the notes right. So this was a new way of doing it for me, and it's really helpful. Having had all the experience of playing for many, many years, it was a good way of doing it.

Lauren: Today on the show we're looking back over 2024, and we wanted to reflect on your year as well. You hosted a really special event called The Floor. It's apparently been a dream of yours to own your own club ever since you discovered Plastic People, and this year you finally got to fulfil it. You had plenty of special guests dropping by, Daphni, John Glacier, Two Shell, Charli xcx and a whole bunch of others, and you played a set that finished with Light of the World's 'London Town', a really lovely jazzy ode to London and its nightlife. What were your intentions for the night, and how did it feel to finally have that ambition realised?

Jamie: It was really special. For a long time I've wanted to own a club, and over the years I've almost bought a couple of spaces to do that in London, and was strongly advised against it by everybody in my life, which I'm grateful for. This was only 10 days, but we spent a long time building out the space, making it sound amazing and feel very intimate. I played 10 nights in a row, and that was enough to satisfy me. It was an incredible experience, extremely exhausting. Then we did it in New York and in LA as well. To be able to do that every night and really get your head into it, and also see all your friends and discover stuff, was very revitalising after finishing a record.

Simon: Your previous album, In Colour, has been described as a nostalgic, rose-tinted homage to a dance-floor era you yourself were too young to experience. Songs like 'Gosh' carry that romance of imagined club experiences and distant pirate radio signals, and part of the record's beauty is that it pictures club culture through the lens of someone who imagined it before they got to experience it. Are you still able to keep that viewpoint, to romanticise club culture, now that you're more in the centre of it all?

Jamie: I think the great thing about dance music is that it's always referencing itself, and moving so fast. It seems to go in these cycles where people reference 20 years ago: new kids going to clubs for the first time, starting to make music, hear that and then do it in a new way, their own way. I love that. It's the fastest-moving genre of all. But on this album, because I'd been doing it for so long, and I was travelling around the world the whole time, I think I wanted to make it less UK-centric and more based on my experiences of dance floors all over the world.

Simon: We understand you even sample ambient sounds from different clubs to locate them in particular places. Is that right?

Jamie: Yeah. It's just a good way to tie things together without anybody noticing, as well. It creates a sort of vibe throughout a record if you texture it with those sorts of things.

Lauren: As a listener, it does become a very transporting experience. Out of curiosity, as someone who has travelled the world in club culture, are you observing shifts over time? Where would you say things are at the moment?

Jamie: It's constantly shifting. And I definitely struggled with it. I was struggling with making the album at this time anyway, and I think part of it was that dance music, which to me was this very personal, special thing that was the coolest thing in the world when I was a kid, had become basically the biggest thing in the world, and was all pop music. I didn't know where my place was in that, and I felt slightly responsible for it as well. So I just had to traverse that. In the end, I basically stopped listening to dance music for a while and just listened to my old records, my parents' records, at home. That gave me the headspace to make something that wasn't within the current climate, I guess. And now there are loads of amazing producers making really cool underground music again, and I'm learning from them.

Lauren: And I guess The Floor was a way of platforming and championing those artists as well.

Jamie: Yeah.

Simon: You've said that, most of the time, feeling good doesn't necessarily lend itself to making good music, and that you have to separate the two. How do you get into a music-making frame of mind? What does that look and feel like?

Jamie: I wish I knew. It's always a challenge. I'm a bit older now, and can't be going out as much as I used to, and obviously it's nice to feel good in your body. But you do need that inspiration, and those moments where you're in a room full of people all listening to the same thing. At least for me, that's super inspiring. So it's all about balance, and I'm always trying to find it. It's especially hard when you're on tour. But I'm working at it, always.

Lauren: We were very curious about the collaborative quality of this record, and the place of friendship at the heart of In Waves. We'd love to talk about local heroes The Avalanches, who of course feature on the record. You've said that listening to their debut, Since I Left You, taught you so much about how to make music. How did it feel to create music with The Avalanches all these years later?

Jamie: It's a dream. I was obsessed with them when I was a kid. I think that album came out when I was like 11, and there wasn't much information about them online. I was trawling the internet for anything, really, and I went and bought all the records they sampled for it and did a really deep dive on that record. This was before you could watch tutorials on YouTube about how to make stuff. So I just listened to that and a few other records and worked out how to do it, and that was the basis for how I learned to produce, which was mostly sampling. Then I got to meet them here. They came to one of my shows years ago. I didn't know they were there until afterwards.

Lauren: That was probably a good thing, right?

Jamie: Yes. At that same show I played a mash-up of a bunch of different tracks from Since I Left You, as an ode to them, not knowing they were there, which was kind of embarrassing.

Simon: I'm sure they appreciated it.

Jamie: But working with them has been great, and I think because I learned how to make music by listening to them, when we make music together it just clicks really easily.

Lauren: What does it look like when you're working together? Did they teach you new techniques, and vice versa? Was it a bit of an exchange?

Jamie: Mostly we would just hang out and talk, and then when we were doing music it would be separate, and they'd send me little videos of what they were doing on the screen. It was very little changes to stuff, because everything they were doing was amazing. So it just worked. It was one of the easiest processes.

Simon: You've described the feeling of a song when you know it's finished as emotional fullness. How do you define that, and what makes a song emotionally full for you?

Jamie: Whenever I talk about this, it just sounds — it's a very hard thing to describe. It's basically just a feeling; that's all I can say about it. I try not to overthink it, because it's quite a rare thing when I get that feeling. It's actually mostly at the beginning of a track, where something happens, usually a mistake, that just makes me feel a certain way, where I know I can turn this into something special.

Lauren: You've spoken a lot about mistakes being really important. Were there any interesting happy accidents that made their way onto this record?

Jamie: So many. I think most of it's an accident.

Lauren: It's being open to the creative process and allowing it to happen.

Jamie: Yes, definitely. Every time I've had an idea and tried to execute it, it's usually pretty dull. But if I just get into that flow state and follow all the mistakes and lose track of time, that's the best.

Simon: As a producer, it must be interesting to hear the evolution of certain songs, too. 'Dafodil' features Panda Bear and John Glacier on the album version, but we understand there's a 20-minute version on a hard drive somewhere, featuring some other guest vocalists. Is that right?

Jamie: A very unfinished 20-minute version, but a lot of people were very kind to deliver verses during lockdown. It was all via text, and I'm so grateful to them all for trying. I'd love to put it together at some point, but that track in particular is very intricate, because it was all to do with chopping these voices up, and the rhythm of the vocals. So it's a long process. The ones that ended up on the album were just the most different to each other, which I thought was interesting.

Simon: Finally, to bring the conversation full circle, we started by talking about surfing. We read that you've developed a really strong interest in surfing over the last 10 years: you had an epiphany in Hawaii back in 2014 and haven't looked back, and you've said you love the trippy, spiritual vibe of surf culture. Does surfing culture offer a shift in perspective for you?

Jamie: Well, I think it's the exact opposite of anything I do professionally, which is perfect for me. I discovered it when I was 25, and it felt like an incredible thing to have a brand new passion at that point in life, when I thought my whole life was about music. I was a city kid, so I wasn't interested in nature at all. It just flipped everything, and now any chance I get, I'll go to a spot.

Simon: So hopefully there'll be some time on this tour.

Jamie: Yeah, I'm hopefully going to get some surfing in Sydney, and then I'm going to Byron for a few days, and that'd be great.

Lauren: Thanks for joining us, Jamie.

Jamie: Thank you.
